specPoints.text: understand how metals can be arranged in a reactivity series based on their reactions with: water; dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid
know the order of reactivity of these metals: potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold

primer.text: From Group 1 (Alkali Metals) you have already seen potassium and sodium react with water, and you know the reactivity series by name from the periodic table work. This note turns those reactions into a measuring tool: comparing how metals behave with cold water and with dilute acids, and using the vigour seen to place them in the order of reactivity.

lessons.title: Reaction with water
sourceHeadings: Reactions of metal with cold water summary table
lessons.opening: The chemistry of metals is studied by watching how they react with water and acids, and the observations place each metal in a reactivity series. With cold water the spread is dramatic: potassium reacts violently, sodium quickly, lithium and calcium less strongly, while magnesium barely stirs in water but reacts rapidly with steam. Zinc and iron react only slowly with steam, and copper shows no reaction at all.
keyPoints: Potassium reacts violently with cold water and sodium reacts quickly.
Lithium and calcium both react less strongly with cold water.
Magnesium barely reacts in cold water, yet responds rapidly to steam.
Zinc and iron react only slowly with steam, and copper shows no reaction.
Calcium with water gives calcium hydroxide and hydrogen: Ca + 2H2O gives Ca(OH)2 + H2.

low.restatement: Drop each metal into cold water and watch: the fiercest frothers are the most reactive. Potassium tops the violence, sodium and then lithium and calcium follow, magnesium waits for steam, and copper does nothing at all.
low.analogy: Like a row of kettles at different heats: the top metals are already boiling over, the middle ones simmer only when steamed, and copper stays stone cold.
low.examPointer: Quote the observations in order from the summary table; the ordering itself is the evidence the question wants.

medium.restatement: Each metal's vigour with cold water fixes its place in the upper part of the series: potassium violent, sodium quick, lithium and calcium progressively gentler. Magnesium's rapid reaction is reserved for steam, zinc and iron manage only slow steam reactions, and copper's lack of reaction places it at the bottom of the tested set.
medium.analogy: Think of a sprint race run on two tracks: cold water times the front runners, while steam is needed to time the middle pack at all.
medium.examPointer: For the calcium equation, check the balancing: one calcium, two waters, one calcium hydroxide and one hydrogen molecule.

check.stem: Which metal reacts violently with cold water?

options.explanation: Potassium heads the cold-water table with a violent reaction, ahead of sodium's quick one.
Magnesium reacts very slowly with cold water; its rapid reaction needs steam.
options.misconception: magnesium's reactivity overstated in cold water

options.explanation: Copper shows no reaction with water at all; it sits at the bottom of the tested metals.
Iron manages only a slow reaction with steam, far short of violent behaviour in cold water.

check.stem: A metal reacts very slowly with cold water but rapidly with steam. Which metal fits this description?

options.explanation: That pair of behaviours is magnesium's signature row in the cold-water summary table.
Calcium reacts less strongly than sodium in cold water, not slowly in water and fast in steam.
Copper reacts with neither water nor steam in this scheme.
Sodium reacts quickly with cold water, which is nothing like the slow-in-water pattern described.

check.stem: What are the products when calcium reacts with cold water?

options.explanation: The equation Ca + 2H2O gives Ca(OH)2 + H2 names both products exactly.
The oxide forms from carbonates on heating; with water the hydroxide is the product.
Water's hydrogen is released as the gas, not its oxygen; oxygen is not produced here.
No carbon dioxide is available to make a carbonate; the metal hydroxide forms instead.

check.stem: Why can the cold-water reactions arrange potassium, sodium, lithium and calcium in order?

options.text: Because each metal's vigour with water differs, and the observations rank them against each other
options.explanation: The series is built by comparing how vigorously each metal reacts, and water alone separates these four.

options.text: Because they all react identically, so only their masses distinguish them
options.explanation: Identical reactions would give no ranking; it is the clear differences in vigour that order them.

options.text: Because water dissolves each metal at a different rate
options.explanation: The metals do not simply dissolve; they react chemically, releasing hydrogen as they form hydroxides.

options.text: Because the water temperature changes for each metal tested
options.explanation: The test keeps conditions comparable; only the metal changes between trials.

check.stem: Copper shows no reaction with water or steam. Where does this place it relative to the other metals tested?

options.text: At the bottom of the tested set, below zinc and iron
options.explanation: No reaction with either water or steam marks the least reactive behaviour in the table.

options.text: Just below potassium, because it also stays shiny
options.explanation: Shininess is not the criterion; the absence of any reaction puts copper last, not near the top.

options.text: Level with magnesium, since both need steam
options.explanation: Magnesium reacts rapidly with steam; copper does not react with steam at all, so they are not level.

options.text: Its position cannot be placed from water reactions
options.explanation: A blank result is still a result: no reaction anywhere places it below every metal that does react.

lessons.title: Reaction with dilute sulfuric or hydrochloric acids
sourceHeadings: Reaction with dilute sulfuric or hydrochloric acids
lessons.opening: Only metals placed above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids, and the more reactive the metal, the more vigorous the reaction. Potassium and sodium are so high that they react explosively with acids, which is far too dangerous to attempt. For the safer metals, every acid reaction follows one pattern: metal plus acid gives a salt plus hydrogen gas.
keyPoints: Only metals above hydrogen in the reactivity series react with dilute acids.
The more reactive the metal, the more vigorous its reaction with the acid.
Potassium and sodium react explosively with acids, so they are too dangerous to try.
The general pattern is metal plus acid giving a salt plus hydrogen.
Magnesium, zinc and iron each form their sulfate with sulfuric acid and their chloride with hydrochloric acid.

low.restatement: A metal reacts with dilute acid only if it sits above hydrogen in the series, and the higher it sits the fiercer the fizzing. The products are always the same in kind: a salt of the metal and hydrogen gas. Every successful fizz is the metal taking hydrogen's place in the acid, which is why position on the ladder decides everything.
low.analogy: Like a ladder over a fixed fence: any metal standing above the hydrogen rung clears it, and the higher it stands, the more spectacularly it lands.
low.examPointer: State the above-hydrogen rule first, then give the salt-plus-hydrogen pattern, and finish with one balanced example; all three lines together earn full marks.

medium.restatement: Dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid tests the metals that outrank hydrogen: their atoms displace hydrogen from the acid, forming the metal's salt while hydrogen bubbles off. Vigour tracks position, from explosive potassium and sodium down to the steady fizz of magnesium, zinc and iron, each making sulfate salts with one acid and chloride salts with the other.
medium.analogy: Picture hydrogen as a flag sitting on one rung of the reactivity ladder: any metal above it snatches the flag from the acid, and the higher the start, the faster the dash.
medium.examPointer: Write one table equation correctly, such as Mg + H2SO4 giving MgSO4 + H2, and generalise the pattern rather than memorising every row.

check.stem: Which metals react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid?

options.text: Only those above hydrogen in the reactivity series
options.explanation: The above-hydrogen rule decides the whole set; metals below it, such as copper, silver and gold, do not react.

options.text: All metals react with dilute acids
options.explanation: Copper's lack of reaction with dilute acids is exactly why it sits below hydrogen.
Magnesium, zinc and iron all react with dilute acids; the rule is about position, not group membership.
That inverts the rule; below-hydrogen metals cannot displace hydrogen from the acid.

check.stem: Why are potassium and sodium never used to make hydrogen from dilute acid in school experiments?

options.text: Because their reactions with acids are explosive
options.explanation: Their position at the top of the series makes the acid reaction too violent to be safe, so gentler metals are used.

options.text: Because they do not react with acids at all
options.explanation: The opposite is true: they react so vigorously that the reaction is dangerous.

options.text: Because they dissolve the glass containers
options.explanation: Glass is unaffected; the hazard is the violence of the reaction itself.

options.text: Because they are too rare to use in schools
options.explanation: Availability is not the reason; the explosive vigour is.

check.stem: What are the products when zinc reacts with dilute sulfuric acid?

options.explanation: Metal plus acid gives salt plus hydrogen, and the salt of zinc with sulfuric acid is zinc sulfate.
Chloride salts come from hydrochloric acid; sulfuric acid makes the sulfate.
No water forms in an acid-metal reaction; the pattern is salt plus hydrogen only.
The gas released is hydrogen, which the metal displaces from the acid.

check.stem: Iron reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid. Which equation matches the pattern?

options.explanation: Iron forms iron(II) chloride with hydrochloric acid, and the hydrogens balance as two HCl giving one H2.
The hydrogens do not balance: one HCl holds one hydrogen, but a hydrogen molecule needs two.
Chlorines do not balance: two on the left cannot give three on the right, and the acid reaction gives iron(II).
That is the correct equation for sulfuric acid, not for the hydrochloric acid named in the question.

check.stem: Copper, silver and gold lie below hydrogen. What does that predict for their reactions with dilute acids?

options.text: They do not react, which is why they resist acids in everyday use
options.explanation: Below-hydrogen metals cannot displace hydrogen from the acid, so no salt-and-hydrogen reaction occurs.

options.text: They react explosively, being dense metals
options.explanation: Density is irrelevant; position below hydrogen means no reaction at all with dilute acids.

options.text: They react only with sulfuric acid
options.explanation: Neither acid works; the position below hydrogen blocks both chloride and sulfate reactions.

options.text: They react only when powdered finely
options.explanation: Surface area speeds reactions up but cannot create one that the reactivity position forbids.

glossary.definition: The ordered list of metals arranged by how readily they react, built from observations with water and acids.
The compound formed when the metal takes hydrogen's place in an acid, such as zinc sulfate.
Water in its hot gaseous state, which reacts with metals too unreactive for cold water.
An acid mixed with much water, such as the dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid used with metals.
The gas released when a metal above hydrogen in the series reacts with water or acid.
